questions.q: In a systematic performance-tuning methodology, what should happen before any tuning change is made?
options: Establish a baseline of normal system behavior so any change's effect can actually be measured
Apply every known best practice immediately, in parallel
Rebuild every index in the database
Restart the SQL Server instance to clear all caches
questions.explain: Without a baseline of what "normal" looks like, there's no way to know whether a change actually helped, made things worse, or had no effect at all — baselining comes first so improvement can be measured, not assumed.

questions.q: Why is a captured performance baseline essential before tuning a system that users describe as "slow"?
options: Baselines are only useful for long-term capacity planning
Without concrete baseline metrics, "slow" is purely subjective; the baseline gives real numbers to compare against once a change is made
Baselines remove the need for any further monitoring once captured
A baseline is only valid if captured exclusively during off-peak hours
questions.explain: "Slow" means different things to different users; a baseline turns that vague complaint into measurable data — response times, wait stats, resource usage — that can be compared before and after a change to prove whether it actually fixed anything.

questions.q: In an execution plan, a large gap between an operator's estimated and actual row counts most often points to what?
options: A hardware failure on the storage subsystem
The query is currently blocked by another session
Stale or inaccurate statistics that misled the optimizer's cardinality estimate
Corruption in tempdb
questions.explain: The optimizer chooses operators and join strategies based on estimated row counts derived from statistics; when those estimates diverge sharply from what actually happened at runtime, outdated or insufficient statistics are the most common culprit.

questions.q: Which query hint forces SQL Server to compile a brand-new plan for a statement instead of reusing whatever plan is currently cached?
options: OPTION (FAST 10)
OPTION (MAXDOP 1)
OPTION (KEEP PLAN)
OPTION (RECOMPILE)
questions.explain: OPTION (RECOMPILE) discards any cached plan and forces a fresh compilation using the current parameter values, which is useful for diagnosing parameter-sensitivity issues, though it adds compilation overhead on every execution.

questions.q: What makes a nonclustered index a "covering index" for a particular query?
options: It contains, as key or included columns, every column the query references — so no lookup into the clustered index is needed
It covers only the columns referenced in the WHERE clause
It must include every column in the underlying table
It is built on the table's primary key
questions.explain: A covering index satisfies the entire query — filtering, joining, and selecting — from the index itself, eliminating the extra Key Lookup into the clustered index that's needed when the index doesn't include every column the query touches.

questions.q: When is a columnstore index typically the better choice over a traditional rowstore index?
options: For OLTP point lookups by primary key
For large analytical or aggregation workloads that scan many rows across relatively few columns
For very small lookup tables
For tables that change on nearly every row, every second
questions.explain: Columnstore's compression and column-oriented storage shine when queries aggregate or scan large volumes of data over a handful of columns — the classic data-warehouse pattern — rather than single-row OLTP lookups, where a traditional rowstore index is usually more efficient.

questions.q: Why does a cursor-based, row-by-row update typically perform worse than an equivalent set-based UPDATE statement over the same rows?
options: Cursors always use less memory than set-based operations
Cursors are required for correctness on large tables
T-SQL doesn't support set-based updates on large tables
The cursor iterates one row at a time, paying per-row overhead, instead of letting the engine optimize processing across the whole set at once
questions.explain: A set-based UPDATE lets the query optimizer build one efficient plan for the entire operation; a cursor forces row-by-row processing with repeated context switches and per-row overhead, which is almost always slower at any meaningful scale.

questions.q: For a large intermediate result set built inside a stored procedure, why might a temp table be preferable to a table variable?
options: Table variables always outperform temp tables regardless of size
Temp tables can never have indexes created on them
Table variables persist data across separate user sessions
Temp tables can have statistics and nonclustered indexes created on them, letting the optimizer make better cardinality estimates for larger row counts
questions.explain: Table variables historically lacked column-level statistics (this is only partially addressed by newer deferred-compilation improvements), which can lead the optimizer to badly underestimate row counts; a temp table behaves more like a regular table, with statistics and indexing, making it a safer choice as data volume grows.

questions.q: After running DBCC SQLPERF('sys.dm_os_wait_stats', CLEAR), how should the wait-stats data collected afterward be interpreted?
options: As wait accumulation over a specific, known time window — better for identifying which waits matter right now than a lifetime total since the last restart
As instantaneous, real-time waits only, with no accumulation
As historical data reaching back years before the clear
As a log of errors only, not wait time
questions.explain: Clearing wait stats and then re-sampling after a defined interval isolates the waits that accumulated during that window, which is far more actionable for diagnosing a current issue than a cumulative total that may span weeks since the last restart and dilute recent problems.

questions.q: A server shows sustained, high SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD waits alongside low PAGEIOLATCH waits. What does this combination suggest?
options: The disk subsystem is the bottleneck
CPU pressure — tasks are voluntarily yielding the scheduler after exhausting their quantum, not waiting on physical I/O
Network latency between application and database is the bottleneck
Memory is significantly over-provisioned
questions.explain: SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD occurs when a task voluntarily yields the CPU after using its full scheduling quantum, which climbs when the CPU itself is saturated; low PAGEIOLATCH waits rule out disk I/O as the current bottleneck, pointing instead toward CPU pressure.

questions.q: Many sessions rapidly creating and dropping temp tables cause contention on which type of tempdb page?
options: Data pages in user databases
The transaction log of user databases
Allocation pages such as PFS, GAM, and SGAM
Pages in the plan cache
questions.explain: Every temp object creation and deallocation touches tempdb's allocation bitmap pages (PFS, GAM, SGAM); under heavy concurrent create/drop activity, many sessions contend for latches on those same pages — the classic reason for splitting tempdb into multiple data files.

questions.q: A query requests a very large memory grant based on inflated cardinality estimates, and sessions start showing RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE waits. What's actually happening?
options: The query is deadlocked with another session
The query is blocked by a row-level lock
The buffer pool is entirely full of dirty pages
The query is waiting for enough workspace (query execution) memory to become free, since its requested grant exceeds what's currently available
questions.explain: RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE waits occur when a query's memory grant request can't be satisfied immediately from the memory grant pool; an inflated cardinality estimate (often from bad statistics or parameter sniffing) can cause SQL Server to request far more memory than the query actually needs, starving other queries.

questions.q: Query Store captures runtime statistics at defined intervals (rather than just a single snapshot). Why does this matter for tuning?
options: It only records a single snapshot taken at server startup
It only tracks whether a query errored, not how long it ran
It only applies to queries executed from within stored procedures
Interval-based capture lets a DBA see how a query's performance trends over time and spot when it regressed, rather than just its current state
questions.explain: By aggregating runtime stats into configurable time intervals and persisting them to disk, Query Store lets a DBA look back and see exactly when a query's duration, CPU, or I/O pattern changed — the foundation for finding and explaining a performance regression.

questions.q: What does forcing a plan in Query Store actually do?
options: It tells SQL Server to reuse a specific, known-good execution plan for that query instead of letting the optimizer potentially pick a regressed one
It permanently prevents the query from being executed again
It disables statistics maintenance for every table the query touches
It automatically converts the ad hoc query into a stored procedure
questions.explain: Plan forcing pins a particular plan_id as the one SQL Server must use for future executions of that query, which is a targeted way to stop a regression caused by the optimizer choosing a worse plan after a recompile, without changing the query text itself.

questions.q: Lowering "cost threshold for parallelism" far below its default of 5 on a typical OLTP system tends to cause what?
options: It prevents any query from ever using parallelism
Many more, smaller queries qualify for parallel execution unnecessarily, increasing CPU overhead and scheduling contention
It has no measurable effect on plan choice
It only changes how backup compression is applied
questions.explain: Cost threshold for parallelism sets the estimated cost above which the optimizer will consider a parallel plan; setting it too low lets cheap, short-running queries go parallel, which adds thread coordination overhead that can hurt throughput on an OLTP workload dominated by short transactions.

questions.q: Why should "max server memory" almost always be configured explicitly on a production SQL Server instance rather than left at its default?
options: The default value is always set too low and hurts performance
It has no real impact on a server dedicated entirely to SQL Server
It only affects how tempdb is sized
The default effectively lets SQL Server consume nearly all available server memory, which can starve the OS and any other processes running on the box
questions.explain: Left unconfigured, SQL Server's buffer pool will grow to use nearly all physical memory, which is fine on a truly dedicated box but can starve the OS, other SQL Server components (like SSAS or SSRS), or co-located applications if memory isn't explicitly capped.

questions.q: Why is a single point-in-time performance snapshot generally insufficient for effective ongoing monitoring?
options: Performance problems are often intermittent or time-dependent, so continuous baseline data over time is needed to recognize a deviation from normal
DMVs already retain unlimited history forever, so snapshots add nothing
A single snapshot is always sufficient for any troubleshooting need
Monitoring tools function correctly without any historical context
questions.explain: Most DMVs reset on restart and reflect only cumulative totals since then; a one-off snapshot can't reveal whether current numbers are normal or abnormal for that server, which is why ongoing baseline collection over time is what actually enables spotting a real deviation.

questions.q: After applying a fix, why validate its effect against the established baseline rather than declaring success because one query ran faster once?
options: Baselines aren't needed anymore once a fix has been applied

A single faster run doesn't confirm the underlying issue is resolved under real production load — it could just reflect a warm cache; comparing metrics against baseline over time gives real confirmation
One successful test run always proves the issue is fully resolved
Validation against a baseline is only necessary for index changes, never for query rewrites
questions.explain: A one-off fast run can be misleading — caches may be warm, or the workload at that moment may be unrepresentative. Comparing wait statistics, resource usage, and query duration against the original baseline over a realistic period of production activity is what actually proves a fix worked.

questions.q: Why document performance-tuning findings even after the immediate issue has been resolved?
options: Documentation is unnecessary once an issue is fixed
It's only required to satisfy a compliance audit, never useful internally
It creates a record that helps recognize recurrence, transfers knowledge to teammates, and justifies the change if it's questioned later
Documentation is only worth writing when a fix fails
questions.explain: A documented record of what the symptom was, what diagnosis pointed to, and what change fixed it means the next person (or the same DBA, months later) doesn't have to re-derive the investigation from scratch if the same pattern reappears.

questions.q: In a performance-tuning capstone presentation, why show wait-statistics data from before and after the fix rather than only the query's new execution time?
options: Wait statistics are irrelevant to proving a fix worked
Execution time alone always tells the complete story of what changed
Wait statistics can't meaningfully be compared across two different time periods
Before-and-after wait stats demonstrate the actual mechanism behind the fix and show that the bottleneck class genuinely changed system-wide, not just for one lucky run
questions.explain: A faster single query run could be a fluke or a warm-cache effect; showing that the dominant wait type shifted (for example, from PAGEIOLATCH-heavy to something far less significant) proves the underlying resource bottleneck was actually addressed, which is a much stronger form of evidence.
